accepted.title: Halo: Campaign Evolved is more successful at being a reinvention of an FPS classic than it is a reproduction - and that needn't be a bad thing
accepted.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Halo: Campaign Evolved.
evidence_points: When Master Chief first sets foot on the unknown ringworld known as Halo, he is fighting for his life. Harried and ambushed by countless enemy ships, Chief's commanding officer scuttles their intergalactic craft upon the ringworld - assuming the human troops will fare better on this structure than face a cold, indifferent death in the vacuum of space. But once they set foot upon Halo, they realise all is not what it seems; here, they are trespassing on the work of a culture that has come before. They are treading on the face of a masterpiece. Interfering with greatness. I can't help but see the parallels to Halo Studios and Bungie.

Halo Studios has an almost impossible task with Halo: Campaign Evolved. They are to infiltrate the world of Bungie's masterwork, and attempt to create a facsimile of it in an inferior engine, with precious few of the original developers to help steer them in the right direction. Conditions are hostile - so hostile, in fact, that even some of the architects of the original game are against Halo Studios . And yet, like one lone armoured supersolider wreaking havoc on a Covenant cruiser, Halo Industries has done something heroic here - it may not be perfect, but Campaign Evolved does manage to do the impossible: it summons the feeling of playing the original again for the first time.

There are plenty of changes, though. You can now aim down sights on every weapon (but taking damage still descopes you, promoting mobility over camping). You can sprint (once again, promoting adaptability and momentum). There are more vehicles dotted around the maps, harkening back to the original Halo's genesis as a 'vehicular combat' strategy game . There are more weapons for you to pilfer from the battlefield, more tactical options at hand for the harder fights. There are dozens of skull modifiers. The later levels have been rethought, stripped of their tedium, packed full of interesting new mechanics.

Thanks to the series changing so much over time - the second game gave you the option to pick up an Elite's energy sword or hijack enemy vehicles, the third game introduced support weapons and equipment - my understanding of what a Halo game feels like has evolved so much since the first game. As a result, Campaign Evolved as a whole feels exactly like Halo now , even if - in the moment-to-moment - it plays like a different game. So going 'back' to the first game where I can sprint, use pretty much any weapon dropped by my enemy (up to and including the Sentinel Lasers of the Forerunner guardians) feels natural. Having recently played Halo: Combat Evolved via the Master Chief Collection, in fact, I felt frustrated by these omissions. The game may be a masterpiece, but it is very much shackled by the architectural constraints of the original Xbox.

But all these iterations come at the cost of something quite nebulous. There was an artistry to the way original designer Jaime Griesemer placed encounters, vehicles, weapons on the map. There was an artisanal feel to the way Halo was crafted; the pace of it remains one of the best FPS experiences to date. Campaign Evolved turns up the dial on fun and approachability, but at the cost of this flow. It's a hard thing to define, but you feel this awkwardness most in the run of missions from The Library to The Maw. Notably, the places Halo Studios has chopped and changed the game the most.

It's not bad, per se, but it's different enough to be jarring. In The Library, for instance, even on Heroic difficulty, you're given a shotgun and encouraged to play the game like an action hero; one-shot killing anything that dares get within spitting distance. You never feel the tension of your ammo running out, rarely feel your armour-plated back pushed against the cold metal wall as 343 Guilty Spark looks on, condescending. It's fun, it gets your heart rate up, but it's not Halo as you remember it. But that's fine, because you can always go and play the Master Chief Collection. Campaign Evolved is trying to give you something different.

The design philosophy is most obvious in the 'Meteorite' package of three new missions that have been added as a prequel to the game, completely original and created by Halo Studios. Taking place a year before The Pillar of Autumn exits slipspace to find the Halo ringworld, the missions follow Master Chief and Sgt. Avery Johnson on a covert operation to infiltrate a Covenant research ship and liberate captured UNSC marines. I rolled my eyes at this when it was announced: 'A prequel trilogy? How droll.' But this trio of missions highlights the differences between Bungie and Halo Studios so well, it almost feels intentional.

Inspired by Troy Denning's Halo books, the writing explores Chief and Johnson's relationship, and introduces a pissed-off Helljumper into the mix to cast a bit of shadow on Chief's heroic status: a bit of in-game colour we're not used to seeing when it comes to Microsoft's de facto mascot. The design of these levels is also curious, if you complete them post-campaign: I think the original Halo is a restrained lesson in FPS design minimalism - you have tools, you have opportunities to use them, you are trusted to do what you will. You're a supersolider, after all. In Meteorite, you are led through a very distinct path, given very specific tools, and are pitted against very specific enemies. At one point, you are literally dumped into a Covenant hunting ground. You must react, not invent. It feels like the Halo Studios philosophy writ large.

But that's not a bad thing. In fact, after inventing my way through bastard-hard skirmishes in the main campaign, this felt like a treat: a curated blockbuster moment, with high production values, clever ideas, and implementation of all the toys you'd want to see from the wider Halo toolkit. Smart, funny, and self-aware. If this is the future of numbered Halo games, count me in. But it's not Halo: Combat Evolved; a game that felt like a lesson in video game design and player agency. And that, really, is the central point of tension in Campaign Evolved. It's a good game, and I'd recommend it, but it feels wrong to wear the skin of probably the best FPS ever made whilst trying to Michael Bay it a bit at the same time.

accepted.title: Halo: Campaign Evolved Review: Rollicking Revival
accepted.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Halo: Campaign Evolved.
evidence_points: Halo: Combat Evolved is a foundational game whose influence and reach are hard to encompass. 25 years ago, that game established an array of mechanics, control systems, story tropes, and gameplay flow that rippled outward across the genre and beyond. In crafting a rebuild, Halo Studios opted to strip out the competitive multiplayer that helped establish part of that reputation, which is a real shame. Even so, Halo: Campaign Evolved does a phenomenal job of capturing what made the 2001 original so much fun while updating certain elements to better suit modern sensibilities. The core game shows its age in some notable ways, but there’s no mistaking the magic that made this formula work all those years ago is still very much intact.

Behind the wall of clever sci-fi world-building, Halo’s triumph has always been its insistent fun at all times, sometimes at the cost of perfect balance or sense. Brightly colored weapon flashes trigger chains of plasma grenade explosions. Warthog vehicles careen over cliffs in improbable arcs. Rocket launchers appear in your path at suspiciously opportune moments for maximum destruction. Enemy grunts are almost gleefully eager to charge into your shooting gallery line-of-fire. The action is constant, the set-piece moments and cinematics are bombastic, and the power fantasy never relents. Halo Studios manages to capture that persistent exuberance, and it’s the highest compliment I can offer for this remake.

I’m also a fan of the selective efforts to update gameplay to contemporary expectations, including the integration of features like sprinting, equipment, and additional aiming options that didn’t come until later installments. Enemies are more dynamic in their actions, especially as they reveal more nuanced and distinct behaviors on higher difficulty levels. Four-player online cooperative play joins the original fun of two-player local. Either way is ideal for sharing the experience with friends.

On the gameplay side, the tough choice not to go further in rebuilding the game keeps the campaign's original flow mostly intact. It must be said, though, that it includes a degree of repetition, backtracking, and narrow-corridor navigation that feels at odds with modern shooters. While it’s no doubt a product of its time, that limitation might help the game feel true to its source material if it didn’t make it feel dated and frustrating to navigate today. I also appreciate the efforts put into offering customization of weapons and armor, and the huge number of unlockable skulls that let you tweak your play experience, including a remix option that offers major changes, like new enemy and weapon placements – a significant bonus to replayability.

The original Halo presented an alluring and mysterious setting that combined alien ruins with Pacific Northwest-inspired natural grandeur, but the level of detail back then simply hadn’t yet caught up with the imagination. That’s resolved here, with a gorgeous visual update that makes the whole campaign pop with excitement. Unfortunately, I encountered several instances of framerate chugging and stuttering when the screen got especially crowded, even if the game otherwise ran smoothly throughout my playthroughs. The remastered audio is stellar, featuring excellently re-recorded dialogue and scoring of all those memorable musical tracks.

For those who, like myself, find some aspects of the campaign to be feeling their age, the three new bonus missions are a welcome addition. This standalone story, set before the events of the main game, gives us more time with fan-favorite Sergeant Johnson, as well as some of the weapons and enemies that came along later in the series. I enjoy the new location aboard a unique Covenant ship, especially the expansive concluding event, though the scope of these three missions feels less impactful overall compared to many Halo adventures over the years.

Master Chief and Cortana’s journey across the ringworld of Halo was an integral experience in my gaming life, and I’m certainly not the only one. Campaign Evolved is a superb update and rebuild of what made the original great, but it stops short of a complete restructuring of that landmark game. Even constrained by some of the features that defined the 2001 classic, this new version nails the roiling current of chaos that made it so fun all those years ago.

accepted.title: Halo: Campaign Evolved Review – Remaster Chief | TheSixthAxis
accepted.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Halo: Campaign Evolved.
evidence_points: It’s no secret that Halo – Xbox ’s leading franchise through the early 2000s – has struggled to gain a footing since Bungie passed the baton on. Just weeks after Halo 3’s launch back in 2007, Activision and Infinity Ward blew up the entire genre with Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare , effectively gluing themselves to the FPS throne thanks to yearly back-to-back releases. In that time, Halo has continued to reinvent itself, the recently renamed Halo Studios (formerly 343 Industries ) pulling the big remake lever to give itself a clean slate, rallying fans both old and new ahead of the series’ next big instalment.

Halo: Campaign Evolved does exactly what it says on the box. This is in many ways a faithful remake and a light reimagining in others, preserving much of the gunplay from the 2001 original Combat Evolved, but feeding in some gameplay elements from later entries, and giving it all an Unreal Engine 5 makeover. Despite being a key ingredient to Halo’s success, online multiplayer isn’t included, though there’s an expanded co-op option and a decent amount of bonus content, including brand new missions that act as a prequel to the main events of the game.

For those completely new to Halo (we imagine there’s a handful of PS5 owners out there) this explosive first chapter pits the plucky, chest-beating marines of the UNSC against the seemingly unstoppable alien alliance known as The Covenant. As they are chased across the galaxy, players assume the role of the hulking, armour-clad super soldier, Master Chief. After awaking from cryostasis, he is forced to flee the UNSC Pillar of Autumn as it is overrun, crash landing on an artificial, ring-shaped world where the fighting continues.

Halo’s story is just as captivating as it was nearly a quarter of a century ago, galvanised by cinematic cutscenes that feature newly recorded dialogue from the game’s original cast. These upgrades to Combat Evolved’s presentation can be felt throughout the remake, though Halo Studios has been careful not to override its art direction – something that the 2011 Anniversary remake was guilty of. The sci-fi visuals have a distinct early 00s look to them, sporting sterile environments that are brought to life by a vibrant mix of bright greens and purples, streaked with bolts of blue and red amidst each chaotic gunfight.

It’s a reminder of how bold and full of character Xbox and PlayStation 2 games looked compared to those from the next console generation, when studios leaned more and more on hyperrealism, swapping rich colour palettes for various shades of brown and grey.

The first person shooter gameplay has also been reworked, lifting a lot from the action from Halo: Reach, yet the changes will feel subtle to those who haven’t recently revisited those classic Halo games. Movement is faster and more fluid, with Master Chief now able to sprint which certainly helps given Halo’s spacious environments. The default control scheme mirrors that adopted by most modern shooters, Campaign Evolved cramming a slew of additional weapons and abilities into the game’s arsenal that weren’t originally there. This, combined with tweaks to stage layouts and the way NPCs behave, helps to add some much needed variety, toning down that inherent gameplay repetitiveness which comes from simply gunning your way from one combat encounter to the next.

In 2001 it was enthralling game design, but FPS campaigns have come a long way in terms of giving players more systems and mechanics to mess with, constantly changing pace while weaving in set piece moments. By contrast, Campaign Evolved can feel plain outdated though intentionally so, to preserve that spirit of the original game.

Despite being created more than two decades later, the new bonus missions pay homage to that classic Halo style. Alongside fan favourite, Sergeant Johnson, players will lead the Master Chief through three levels that take place a year before the events of Halo: Combat Evolved. They slot in nicely with the rest of the game, introducing new enemies and environments while expanding Halo’s Covenant lore with a satisfying, never-before-seen chapter in Master Chief’s story, written by long-time series veteran, Troy Denning. The cutscenes are particularly worthwhile, even if they’re occasionally spliced with some hokey Marvel-esque banter between characters.

Beyond the core campaign and these bonus missions, there isn’t much for those who don’t consider themselves hardcore Halo fans. By collecting Skulls – first introduced in Halo 3 – you can go back and replay missions, applying modifiers that introduce new challenges, or elements such as a third person camera. Skulls are completely missable, but add some much-needed zaniness while dialling up the fun factor, especially in co-op. Speaking of which, Halo: Campaign Evolved allows you to play with a buddy in local split-screen or create online squads of up to four players from your friends list, when the original was limited to two. The complete absence of online PvP is certainly a letdown, though we imagine Microsoft is reluctant to further fragment the remaining Halo multiplayer community which is already split between Halo: Infinite and The Master Chief Collection .
